name: AI and Machine Learning in Network Operations
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Predictive and generative AI in network operations: how models learn, forecast and flag trouble, and how to verify what they say.

lesson.intro: Networks produce more telemetry than any team can read, and AI turns it into warnings, answers and drafts. The CCNA asks you to tell predictive from generative AI, know how machine learning learns, and spot where AI can mislead you.
objectives: Distinguish predictive from generative AI with operations examples
Describe supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and training versus inference
Explain baselines, anomaly detection, forecasting, failure prediction and alert correlation
Write a useful prompt for an assistant and verify its output
Identify AI risks such as hallucination and prompt injection, and the guardrails that manage them

sections.title: AI, machine learning and why operations needs them
sections.key: Predictive AI analyzes data to detect, classify and forecast; generative AI creates new content such as summaries and draft configurations.
sections.body:
At 9:02 on a Monday a campus network raises 1,400 alerts. Somewhere in the pile is one cause: a failed uplink on a distribution switch. AI in operations promises to find it in seconds, and better, to have warned you on Friday that its optic was degrading.

[[visual]]

A rule says "alert if CPU is above 90 percent". A learned model says "this CPU pattern is unusual for this router at this hour". The blueprint names two families of AI by what they do:

[[visual 2]]

Both need what controller-based networking provides: lots of centralized, structured data from many devices, plus serious compute. That is why AI features live in platforms such as Catalyst Center, cloud dashboards and analytics services, not on individual switches.

items.title: Predictive AI
points: Analyzes historical and current data
"This traffic is abnormal"
"This link will be full in six weeks"
"This switch is likely to fail"

items.title: Generative AI
points: Produces new content from a prompt
"Summarize last night's outage"
"Draft an ACL that blocks Telnet from the guest VLAN"
"Explain this `show` output"

sections.tip: Exam shortcut: predictive AI detects and forecasts; generative AI creates.
sections.pitfall: Generative AI is not a more advanced kind of predictive AI. They answer different questions, and one platform often uses both: a predictive model detects an issue and a generative assistant explains it.

check.question: A platform warns that a WAN link will likely exceed 90 percent utilization within five weeks, based on six months of traffic history. Which kind of AI is this?
choices: Generative AI
A static threshold rule
Predictive AI
Reinforcement learning
check.explanation: Forecasting a future value from historical trends is predictive AI. Generative AI would create content such as a summary, and a static threshold only fires once the limit is crossed.

sections.title: How machines learn
sections.key: Labeled examples make it supervised learning, no labels make it unsupervised, and actions that earn rewards or penalties make it reinforcement learning.
sections.body:
A machine learning model is a function with many adjustable parameters, tuned until its outputs fit the data. Each example is described by **features**, the measurable inputs: interface errors per minute, optic temperature, CPU load, time of day.

[[visual]]

Labels are often the expensive part. That is why unsupervised anomaly detection suits networks: nobody labels every flow as good or bad. Reinforcement learning experiments as it learns, so production networks allow it only within strict limits.

Three problem types cover most uses:

[[visual 2]]

For the CCNA you need no math, only this matching.

rows: Labeled examples: each record includes the right answer
Predict optic failure from history labeled "failed within 30 days" or not; classify flows from labeled captures
Unlabeled data; finds structure by itself
Group clients that behave alike; learn normal and flag what does not fit
Actions that earn rewards or penalties, by trial and feedback
Try Wi-Fi channel and power plans, rewarded for better client experience
Is this flow voice, video or backup? Will this optic fail?
Next month's utilization of a link, in percent

sections.tip: Labels make it supervised. No labels make it unsupervised. Rewards make it reinforcement.
sections.pitfall: Anomaly detection is usually unsupervised: it learns normal behavior without anyone labeling every fault or attack. Do not assume detection always needs labeled examples of each problem.

check.question: A team trains a model on 50,000 past support tickets, each tagged with its confirmed root cause, so it can suggest causes for new tickets. Which type of learning is this?
choices: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Generative learning
check.explanation: Every training example carries the correct answer (the root cause label), which is the definition of supervised learning. Unsupervised learning would have no labels, and reinforcement learning needs actions and rewards.

sections.title: Training, inference and data quality
sections.key: Training learns from historical data and is compute-heavy; inference applies the trained model to new data continuously. Both are only as good as the data.
sections.body:
A model's life has two very different phases:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Garbage in, garbage out. Network data fails in specific ways:

[[visual 3]]

Models make two kinds of mistakes. A **false positive** flags a problem that is not there; too many and people ignore the alerts. A **false negative** misses a real problem. Tuning to reduce one usually raises the other.

The playground trains a baseline from history, then runs inference on new samples.

items.title: Training
points: Adjusts its parameters on large amounts of historical data
Compute-heavy and slow, often in the cloud on specialized hardware
Once or periodically, never per packet

items.title: Inference
points: New data in, prediction or answer out
Far cheaper and fast
Runs continuously: scoring each telemetry sample, answering a chat question

steps.label: Clean it, and label it if needed
Validate it on data it has not seen

rows: **Gaps and coarse samples**: devices that stop reporting, counters reset at reload, SNMP polls every five minutes
Short bursts never seen. Streaming telemetry at finer granularity helps
Events correlated in the wrong order, so NTP is an AI prerequisite
**Unrepresentative history**: a baseline learned in a holiday week, during an outage or a faulty nightly flood
Normal days flagged as anomalies, and real faults treated as normal
**Drift**: a new application, a merger, a move to the cloud
Yesterday's normal is wrong until the model is retrained

sections.tip: Training learns from the past; inference applies what was learned to the present.
sections.pitfall: If device clocks are not synchronized with NTP, an AI correlating events across devices can put the effect before the cause. Data hygiene is not optional.

activity.title: Learn a baseline, then score new data
activity.prompt: Run it. The first lines are training and the scoring loop is inference. Notice that the static 90 Mbps rule catches nothing, while the learned baseline flags both the spike and the link that went quiet. Then change the limit and the training data, and watch false positives and false negatives appear.

props.code:
from statistics import mean, pstdev

# Training data: uplink load (Mbps) at 9 a.m. on twelve recent weekdays
history = [42, 45, 39, 47, 44, 41, 46, 43, 40, 48, 44, 42]

# Training: learn what normal looks like
baseline = mean(history)
spread = pstdev(history)
print(f"Learned baseline {baseline:.1f} Mbps, spread {spread:.1f}")

# Inference: score each new sample against the learned baseline
def score(sample, limit=3):
    z = (sample - baseline) / spread
    verdict = "ANOMALY" if abs(z) > limit else "normal"
    return f"{sample:>3} Mbps  z={z:+5.1f}  {verdict}"

new_samples = [44, 51, 88, 12]
for s in new_samples:
    print(score(s))

# A static rule for comparison
STATIC_LIMIT = 90
print("Static rule flags:", [s for s in new_samples if s > STATIC_LIMIT])
props.task: Change limit=3 to limit=2 and rerun: what happens to the 51 Mbps sample? Then add a holiday reading of 5 to the history list and see how one unrepresentative training value shifts the baseline and the verdicts.

check.question: A vendor trains its anomaly model once a month in its cloud, and your controller scores live telemetry against it every minute. What is the every-minute scoring called?
choices: Training
Labeling
Reinforcement
Inference
check.explanation: Applying an already trained model to new data is inference. Training is the monthly learning step, done separately and far less often.

sections.title: Predictive AI: baselines, anomalies and forecasts
sections.key: A learned baseline knows what is normal for each device at each hour, so it flags unusual drops and off-hours spikes that a static threshold never sees.
sections.body:
Traditional monitoring uses **static thresholds**: alert when CPU passes 90 percent. A threshold high enough to stay quiet during nightly backups misses a link at 40 percent when it should be at 5, and it never notices a busy link going quiet.

[[visual]]

Predictive AI replaces fixed limits with learned behavior:

[[visual 2]]

An anomaly is a lead, not a verdict: it might be an attack, a failure or just a new backup job. Catalyst Center Assurance, SD-WAN and Meraki analytics use these techniques; the exam needs the techniques, not product details.

visual.title: Uplink traffic: static rule vs learned baseline
rows: ANOMALY: far above normal for Sunday night
Learns normal for each device, interface, site and client type, by time of day and day of week
Flags departures from the baseline: a spike, a drop to zero, slow DHCP at one access point, a host suddenly contacting hundreds of ports or a new external peer
Projects trends: "this WAN link reaches 85 percent in six weeks", "this DHCP scope runs out next month"
Spots early signs such as rising CRC errors or falling optic power, so parts are replaced in a maintenance window
SD-WAN picks paths from predicted, not just current, loss and latency

sections.tip: If a question contrasts AI with alerting when a value crosses a fixed number, the AI answer is about learned, context-aware baselines.
sections.pitfall: An anomaly is not automatically a fault or an attack. Treat it as a question to investigate, and confirm or dismiss it so the system improves.

check.question: Why can a learned baseline catch problems that a static threshold misses?
choices: It ignores the time of day, which makes it simpler
It uses higher limits than any engineer would set
It only alerts after a device has already failed
It knows what is normal for that device at that time, so it can flag unusual drops as well as spikes
check.explanation: A baseline is specific to the device, metric and time, so a value that is harmless at 9 a.m. can be flagged at 3 a.m., and traffic that suddenly stops is noticed. A fixed threshold only fires when one number is crossed.

sections.title: Predictive AI at work: forecasts, failing hardware, endpoints
sections.key: Forecasts buy lead time, failure prediction swaps parts before outages, and classifiers label endpoints and encrypted flows, but each is a probability built on past data.
sections.body:
**Capacity forecasting.** Fit a trend through each month's busiest-hour utilization and project when it crosses your upgrade level. A new circuit takes months to order, so "85 percent by spring" in October beats an alert in spring. This is regression; real platforms add seasonality and a confidence range.

[[visual]]

**Failure prediction.** Hardware rarely dies without warning. A model that saw these patterns before past failures opens a ticket while the device still works:

[[visual 2]]

**Classifying endpoints and traffic.** Cisco's AI Endpoint Analytics in Catalyst Center labels unregistered cameras, badge readers and printers from their traffic, so policy follows device type. Encrypted Traffic Analytics learns from metadata of encrypted flows, such as packet lengths and timing early in the session, to spot malware without decrypting.

A forecast assumes the future looks like the past, and a classification is a probability: confirm it before applying high-impact policy.

visual.title: When does the WAN link fill up?
visual.result: Crosses 85% in month 16: eight months to order and install a bigger circuit

visual.title: Early warnings a failure model learns
rows: CRC and input errors rising daily
Dirty or failing fiber or optic
Fan speed and temperature creeping up

sections.tip: The value of a forecast is lead time: it turns an outage you react to into an upgrade you plan.
sections.pitfall: A forecast extrapolates the past. Events it never saw, such as a new office, a merger or a new application, can make it badly wrong, so revisit forecasts when the business changes.

activity.title: Forecast when a link fills up
activity.prompt: Run it. Training fits a straight line through eight months of history; inference projects it forward until it crosses 85 percent. Then make the last two months 75 and 82, as if a new application went live, and rerun: the forecast jumps from eight months away to three. Ask yourself whether a straight line really explains that jump.

props.code:
# Busiest-hour utilization (%) of a WAN link, last 8 months
months = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
util = [52, 54, 57, 58, 61, 63, 66, 68]

# Training: fit a straight line through the history (least squares)
n = len(months)
mx = sum(months) / n
my = sum(util) / n
slope = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(months, util)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in months)
intercept = my - slope * mx
print(f"Learned trend: {slope:+.2f} points per month")

# Inference: project forward until the upgrade threshold
THRESHOLD = 85
month = months[-1]
while intercept + slope * month < THRESHOLD:
    month += 1
print(f"Forecast reaches {THRESHOLD}% in month {month}, {month - months[-1]} months from now")

for m in range(9, 13):
    print(f"month {m:2d}: {intercept + slope * m:5.1f}%")
props.task: Change util to [52, 54, 57, 58, 61, 63, 75, 82] and rerun. Then set THRESHOLD = 90 and see how much warning you would get.

check.question: A forecast built from the last eight months says a WAN link reaches 85 percent in month 16. In month 9 the company opens a new office whose traffic will use that link. What should the team do?
choices: Trust the forecast, because it was trained on real data
Treat the forecast as outdated and rebuild it with the new demand, because the trend cannot know about an event missing from its data
Switch the model to generative AI so it can imagine the new traffic
Ignore capacity until the link actually reaches 85 percent
check.explanation: A trend model projects the past forward. A step change in demand that was not in its training data breaks that assumption, so the forecast must be revisited with the new information. Waiting for the threshold throws away the lead time that makes forecasting useful.

sections.title: AIOps: from 1,400 alerts to one incident
sections.key: AIOps deduplicates and correlates alert floods by timing and topology, ranks the likely root cause, suggests an action, and automates only low-risk fixes.
sections.body:
**AIOps** (AI for IT operations) applies these techniques to the operations workflow: collect telemetry, logs and events, make sense of them, and help people or automation act. Back to Monday at 9:02:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The goal is not to remove engineers. It cuts alert fatigue, shortens the time to find and fix problems, and saves human attention for judgment. Most teams start with read-only recommendations and widen what the system may do as it earns trust.

steps.label: Noise reduction and deduplication
steps.detail: 300 identical "AP unreachable" alerts become one item

steps.label: Correlation
steps.detail: Alerts at the same moment on topologically connected devices become one incident

steps.label: Root cause analysis
steps.detail: dist-sw2's uplink failed at 09:01:58, two seconds before the rest; the others are symptoms

steps.label: Recommended action
steps.detail: Check the optic, whose receive power fell for a week, with evidence on the ticket

steps.label: Automated remediation, with guardrails
steps.detail: Low-risk fixes such as bouncing a stuck port can run alone; riskier ones wait for approval

items.title: Before
points: 09:01:58 dist-sw2 Te1/1/1 down
09:02:00 AP-2F-14 unreachable
09:02:01 acc-sw2-3 lost uplink
09:02:03 DHCP timeouts on VLAN 20

items.title: After correlation
points: Probable cause: dist-sw2 Te1/1/1 down at 09:01:58
Impact: 3 access switches, 61 APs, about 900 clients
Evidence: optic receive power falling for 7 days
Suggested: replace the optic, test the fiber

sections.tip: Correlation needs topology and accurate timestamps. That is why controllers and NTP make AIOps work.
sections.pitfall: Correlation is not proof of causation. Events that happen together may share a cause neither of them explains, so verify a suggested root cause before acting on it.

check.question: What does correlation in an AIOps platform do with the alerts caused by a single failed uplink?
choices: Deletes them so engineers are not disturbed
Raises every alert to critical severity
Forwards each alert to a different team
Groups the related alerts into one incident and points to the likely root cause
check.explanation: Correlation uses timing and topology to see that hundreds of alerts are symptoms of one event, so engineers work one incident instead of hundreds of tickets.

sections.title: Generative AI assistants
sections.key: An assistant explains, drafts and summarizes from patterns it learned. Grounding it in your network's data makes it relevant, and agents that act on their own raise the stakes.
sections.body:
Generative AI reaches engineers mostly as an **assistant**: a chat window in a management platform, code editor or general tool, backed by a large language model.

[[visual]]

An LLM is trained on huge amounts of text to predict likely next words. It does not look up facts or run commands unless the tool around it does, and it knows nothing about your network. **Grounding** fixes that:

[[visual 2]]

**Agentic AI** plans several steps and calls tools itself: it runs show commands through an API, reads the results, and proposes or even makes a change. That saves time and raises the stakes, so agents get read-only tools first and need approval before any change.

Treat output as a draft from a fast, well-read colleague who has never seen your network and is sometimes confidently wrong.

rows: "Which sites had the most failed onboarding yesterday?" becomes queries or API calls, then a summary
What a `show` output, log message or configuration diff means
A configuration snippet, ACL, Ansible playbook, Python script, change plan or report
Hundreds of log lines or a long ticket history, condensed into what happened and what is open

steps.label: The model answers from your question plus that data

sections.tip: Ask the assistant to explain its answer and show the data it used. A draft you understand is a draft you can verify.
sections.pitfall: Fluency is not accuracy. Well-formatted, confident output can still contain a wrong command, a wrong value or an invented feature.

check.question: Which task is the best fit for a generative AI assistant in network operations?
choices: Summarizing a long incident timeline into a short report for an engineer to review
Forwarding packets faster than the switch ASIC
Guaranteeing that a configuration is correct before deployment
Replacing the change approval process
check.explanation: Summarizing and drafting are what generative models do well, with a person reviewing the result. They cannot guarantee correctness, and they do not belong in the forwarding path or in place of change control.

sections.title: Using an assistant well: context in, evidence out
sections.key: Give the assistant context (platform, goal, scope, constraints, output), never secrets, then verify its draft against the device, a lab test and the result.
sections.body:
Ask "write an ACL to block Telnet" and you get a generic answer, perhaps applied to an interface the model guessed. Supply what a colleague would need:

[[visual]]

Then treat the answer as a draft and verify it in layers:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

Ask the assistant to list its assumptions (interface names, version, existing configuration): that is where errors hide. And this is why the CCNA still expects you to know the commands: you are the one who notices a missing `permit ip any any` or an ACL in the wrong direction.

visual.title: A useful prompt
rows: "Block Telnet from guest VLAN 50 (10.50.0.0/24) to anywhere; allow everything else"
"Named ACL, applied inbound on interface Vlan50"
"The commands, then one line explaining each"
visual.caption: Leave secrets out: the assistant never needs your enable secret or SNMP communities to draft an ACL.

steps.label: Read it
steps.detail: Addresses, wildcard masks, interface names, direction, and what the implicit deny will do

steps.label: Check the device, not the assistant
steps.detail: Show commands: does Vlan50 exist? Is another ACL already applied?

steps.label: Test it
steps.detail: Lab or simulator, then a change window with a rollback plan

steps.label: Confirm the result
steps.detail: `show access-lists` counters; test what should be blocked and what should still work

sections.code:
ip access-list extended GUEST-NO-TELNET
 deny   tcp 10.50.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq telnet
 permit ip any any
!
interface Vlan50
 ip access-group GUEST-NO-TELNET in
!
SW1# show access-lists GUEST-NO-TELNET
Extended IP access list GUEST-NO-TELNET
    10 deny tcp 10.50.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq telnet (12 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (8812 matches)
sections.tip: Context in, evidence out: platform, goal, scope and constraints in the prompt; explanations and assumptions in the answer.
sections.pitfall: Do not verify an AI answer by asking the same AI whether it is right. Check against the device, the documentation and a test.

check.question: Which prompt is most likely to get a usable configuration draft from an assistant?
choices: Write an ACL to block Telnet
Write the best possible ACL and be accurate
Catalyst 9300 on IOS XE 17.9: block Telnet from VLAN 50 (10.50.0.0/24) to anywhere, allow all else, named ACL inbound on Vlan50, explain each line
Here is our full running-config with passwords; fix our security
check.explanation: The third prompt gives the platform, exact scope, constraints and the output wanted, so the draft can be specific and checkable. Asking for accuracy adds nothing, and pasting a config with secrets into an assistant risks leaking them.

sections.title: Risks, guardrails and the human in the loop
sections.key: Hallucination, bad data, privacy leaks and prompt injection are the main AI risks, so a qualified person verifies, tests and approves AI output before production.
sections.body:
AI makes mistakes differently from people, and safe use starts with knowing how.

[[visual]]

A classic hallucination: asked to permit 192.168.10.0/24, an assistant wrote a subnet mask where IOS expects a wildcard. IOS accepts the line, and it matches the wrong addresses.

[[code]]

The guardrails are the disciplines that make any automation safe:

- A qualified person verifies AI output and stays **accountable** for the change.
- Generated changes take the normal path: lab or dry run, peer review, change control, version control and a rollback plan.
- **Least privilege**: AI tools start read-only, with approval before any change.
- Use approved tools, and strip secrets before sharing anything.
- Log suggestions, approvals and actions; confirm or reject AI-raised issues so models improve.

Your networking knowledge is what tells a good suggestion from a dangerous one.

rows: Plausible, confident output that is false: a command your platform lacks, a wrong default, an invented RFC, a subtle logic error
Predictions from bad, sparse or unrepresentative data, with no warning that the model is guessing
A running-config pasted into a public tool leaks passwords, keys, SNMP communities, addressing and topology
Text the AI reads (a log message, ticket or web page) carries instructions meant to steer it; it must stay data, never commands
No reason given for a conclusion; gaps in training data show up as bias

sections.code:
! Asked: permit 192.168.10.0/24 only
! AI draft (IOS accepts it, but it is wrong):
access-list 10 permit 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
! As a wildcard, 255.255.255.0 ignores the
! first three octets: it matches any x.x.x.0
!
! Correct, with a wildcard mask:
access-list 10 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
sections.tip: Rule of thumb: AI can draft, explain and suggest; a qualified person verifies, tests and approves.
sections.pitfall: The most dangerous AI output is not obviously broken; it is almost right. Check values, masks, interface names and scope, not just syntax.

check.question: An engineer wants to paste a router's full running-config into a free public chatbot to ask why OSPF will not form. What is the main concern?
choices: The chatbot cannot read Cisco syntax
The config can expose secrets such as passwords, keys and SNMP communities, plus internal addressing, to a third party
OSPF configurations are too long for AI tools
Public chatbots only answer questions about programming
check.explanation: A running-config holds credentials and a map of the network. Sending it to an unapproved third-party service risks leaking both. Use an approved tool and remove secrets first.

keyTerms.definition: AI that learns patterns from data instead of following rules written by people.
AI that analyzes data to detect, classify and forecast, such as anomalies, capacity and failures.
AI that creates new content, such as text, code or configurations, in response to a prompt.
Learning from labeled examples, where each record includes the correct answer.
Finding structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters or anomalies.
Learning by trying actions and receiving rewards or penalties.
The compute-heavy phase where a model learns its parameters from historical data.
Using a trained model on new data to produce a prediction or output.
A learned picture of normal behavior for a device or metric, often by time of day and day of week.
Flagging behavior that departs from the learned baseline.
Applying AI to IT operations: noise reduction, correlation, root cause analysis and guided or automated remediation.
Plausible, confident output from a generative model that is false or invented.
Supervised problem types: classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number.
Projecting utilization trends forward to predict when a link or resource needs an upgrade.
A false positive flags a problem that is not there; a false negative misses a real one.
A generative model trained on huge amounts of text to predict likely next words; the engine behind most AI assistants.
Grounding an LLM by retrieving relevant data, such as your inventory or documentation, and supplying it with the question.
An AI system that plans steps and calls tools or APIs to act, which calls for scoped permissions and approvals.
Instructions hidden in text an AI reads, such as logs or tickets, meant to steer what it does.

summary: Predictive AI detects and forecasts; generative AI creates summaries, explanations and drafts.
Supervised uses labels, unsupervised finds structure without them, reinforcement learns from rewards.
Training is compute-heavy learning from history; inference applies the model to new data, and both need clean, timestamped data.
Learned baselines catch what static thresholds miss, forecasts buy lead time, and AIOps correlates alert floods.
Give an assistant context, keep secrets out, and verify against the device, a lab test and change control.
A qualified person verifies and approves AI output, because hallucinations look as confident as facts.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a manager who wants to let the AI run the network what predictive and generative AI can each do for the operations team, how a model learns and is then used, and which safeguards you would insist on before AI output reaches production.

questions.question: What is the main difference between predictive AI and generative AI?
choices: Predictive AI analyzes data to detect and forecast; generative AI creates new content such as text or configurations
Predictive AI is used only for wireless networks; generative AI only for routing
Generative AI needs no training data, while predictive AI does
They are two names for the same technique
questions.explanation: Predictive AI answers what is normal, what is wrong and what will happen. Generative AI produces new output in response to a prompt. Both are trained on large amounts of data.

questions.question: An engineer types "summarize every change made to the core switches this week" into a management platform and gets back a paragraph. Which kind of AI wrote the paragraph?
choices: Predictive AI
Generative AI
A static threshold rule
Unsupervised clustering
questions.explanation: Producing new text from a prompt is generative AI. Predictive AI would classify or forecast rather than write a summary.

questions.question: Match each scenario to the kind of AI or learning it describes.

pairs.left: Forecast that a WAN link will be full in six weeks
Draft an ACL from a plain-English request
Learn to predict optic failures from history labeled failed or not failed
Group clients with similar behavior when no labels exist
Improve a radio channel plan by trying settings and receiving a score

questions.explanation: Forecasting is predictive, creating text is generative, labeled examples mean supervised, structure without labels means unsupervised, and actions with rewards mean reinforcement learning.

questions.question: A model learns normal traffic patterns from months of unlabeled flow records and flags flows that do not fit. Which type of learning is this most likely?
choices: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
A rule-based expert system
questions.explanation: No labels were provided; the model found the structure of normal traffic by itself and flags outliers. That is unsupervised anomaly detection.

questions.question: What makes a machine learning problem supervised?
choices: A human supervises the model while it runs inference
The model receives rewards for good actions
The model runs on the supervisor engine of a chassis switch
The training data includes the correct answer, or label, for each example
questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns a mapping from features to known answers. Rewards for actions describe reinforcement learning, and supervision of the running model is not what the term means.

questions.question: Which description fits reinforcement learning?
choices: A model learns from examples that each include the right answer
A model groups data points that have no labels
An agent takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and learns which actions work best
A model generates text that continues a prompt
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning is trial and feedback: actions earn rewards or penalties, and the agent shifts toward actions that pay off. Because it learns by experimenting, it needs strict limits on a production network.

questions.question: What is inference?
choices: Collecting and labeling historical data
Using a trained model to make predictions or generate output from new data
Adjusting a model's parameters using historical data
Deleting a model that has drifted
questions.explanation: Inference is the use phase: new data in, prediction or answer out. Adjusting parameters on historical data is training.

questions.question: Why is training usually done in the cloud or on dedicated hardware, while inference can run continuously inside a controller?
choices: Inference needs more data than training
Training must happen on every packet
Training processes huge amounts of data and is compute-heavy, while running a trained model on new data is comparatively cheap
Inference cannot run on servers
questions.explanation: Learning the parameters takes large datasets and heavy compute, so it is done periodically on capable hardware. Applying the learned model to each new sample is light enough to run all the time.

questions.question: Put the machine learning lifecycle in order.
items: Clean the data and label it if needed
Validate the model on data it has not seen
Monitor accuracy and retrain when it drifts
questions.explanation: Data comes first, training learns from it, validation checks the model on unseen data, deployment puts it to work, and monitoring catches drift that calls for retraining.

questions.question: A traffic baseline was learned during a month when a misconfigured backup job flooded a link every night. The job has now been fixed. What is the likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because models ignore unusual training data
The model corrects itself instantly
The link starts dropping packets
Normal quiet nights may now be flagged as anomalies, and a real nightly flood may be missed, until the model retrains on clean data
questions.explanation: The model learned the flood as normal. Quiet nights now look like a drop (false positives), and a genuine flood looks normal (false negatives). Unrepresentative training data has to be cleaned out and the model retrained.

questions.question: An AIOps platform keeps naming a symptom as the root cause because the switch that really failed has a clock five minutes behind. What should the team fix first?
choices: Increase the SNMP polling interval
Synchronize every device with NTP so event timestamps line up
Disable syslog on the failed switch
Switch the model from supervised to reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis relies on the order of events across devices. With a skewed clock the real cause appears to happen after its symptoms. NTP fixes the data, and better data fixes the analysis.

questions.question: An anomaly detector flags the routine Saturday backup as an attack every week. What kind of error is this?
choices: False positive
False negative
True positive
Hallucination
questions.explanation: Flagging something harmless as a problem is a false positive. A false negative would be missing a real attack. Hallucination describes generative models inventing content.

questions.question: What is a baseline in AI-driven network monitoring?
choices: The minimum IOS version allowed on the network
The first configuration saved on a device
A learned picture of normal behavior for a device or metric, often by time of day and day of week
A fixed alert threshold set by the vendor
questions.explanation: A baseline is learned from history and reflects context such as time and day. Anomaly detection compares new data against it.

questions.question: What happens in this situation?
questions.code:
Interface Gi0/1 traffic, Sunday 03:00
Learned normal for this hour:  2 to 6 Mbps
Observed:                      41 Mbps
Static alert threshold:        90 Mbps
choices: Only the static threshold raises an alert
Only the learned baseline flags it as an anomaly; the static threshold stays silent
Both raise alerts
Neither raises an alert, because 41 Mbps is well below the threshold
questions.explanation: 41 Mbps never crosses the fixed 90 Mbps limit, but it is many times the learned normal for 3 a.m. on a Sunday, so only the baseline-based detector notices.

questions.question: Which three are uses of predictive AI in network operations? Choose three.
choices: Forecasting when a link will run out of capacity
Detecting unusual traffic compared with a learned baseline
Predicting hardware failure from rising error counts
Writing a post-incident report from a prompt
Drafting a new Ansible playbook from a description
questions.explanation: Forecasting, anomaly detection and failure prediction all analyze data to detect or predict. Writing reports and drafting playbooks create new content, which is generative AI.

questions.question: Why is an AI-flagged anomaly best treated as a lead rather than a verdict?
choices: Anomaly detectors are always wrong
A departure from normal can come from an attack, a failure or legitimate new activity, so someone must determine the cause
Anomalies can only be caused by hardware failures
Baselines never change, so anomalies are meaningless
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection says something is different, not why. A new application, a backup job or a real attack can all look unusual, so investigation decides what it is.

questions.question: Why does an AIOps platform group 300 "AP unreachable" alerts with one "uplink down" alert?
choices: They all share the same severity level
All AP alerts are grouped together regardless of timing
The uplink alert was the most recent one
They occurred together on topologically connected devices, so they are most likely one incident with one root cause
questions.explanation: Correlation combines timing and topology: the access points all depend on that uplink, and their alerts followed its failure within seconds.

questions.question: A team wants AI to fix network problems automatically. Which approach follows good practice?
choices: Let the AI apply any change it recommends, since it has seen more data than any engineer
Never use AI recommendations at all
Allow automatic remediation only for well-understood, low-risk actions, and require human approval for riskier changes
Allow automatic changes only outside business hours, with no logging
questions.explanation: Closed-loop automation should start narrow and earn trust: safe, well-understood fixes can run automatically, risky ones need approval, and everything is logged.

questions.question: What is a main goal of AIOps?
choices: Replace routing protocols with machine learning
Remove the need for monitoring data
Mark every alert as critical
Reduce alert noise and shorten the time to find and fix problems
questions.explanation: AIOps turns floods of alerts into a few correlated incidents with likely causes, so teams detect and repair problems faster. It depends on more and better data, not less.

questions.question: What term describes a generative AI model confidently producing output that is false or invented?
questions.explanation: Hallucinations look as fluent and confident as correct answers, which is why AI-generated configurations must be verified.

questions.question: An AI assistant drafted this configuration. What is wrong with it?
questions.code:
! Request: allow only hosts in 172.16.20.0/24 to reach the VTY lines
access-list 15 permit 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0
line vty 0 4
 access-class 15 in
choices: access-class must be applied out, not in
Standard ACLs cannot be used on VTY lines
The ACL uses a subnet mask where IOS expects a wildcard mask; it should be 0.0.0.255
ACL number 15 is reserved for IPv6
questions.explanation: IOS reads 255.255.255.0 as a wildcard: ignore the first three octets and match a last octet of 0. The line is accepted but permits the wrong hosts. Applying a standard ACL inbound on VTY lines with access-class is correct.

questions.question: Before sharing device output with an AI tool, what should an engineer do?
choices: Convert the output to JSON so it is encrypted
Use an approved tool and remove secrets such as passwords, keys and SNMP communities
Nothing, because AI tools never store their input
Share only the startup-config, because it contains no secrets
questions.explanation: Configs contain credentials and a map of the network, and the startup-config holds the same secrets as the running-config. Approved tools and stripped secrets keep the data from leaking. JSON is a format, not encryption.

questions.question: Which three are real risks of using AI in network operations? Choose three.
choices: Hallucinated commands or values that look correct
Predictions skewed by poor or unrepresentative training data
Sensitive configuration data leaking to a third party
AI models are unable to read syslog messages
Generative AI can only write text in English
questions.explanation: Hallucination, bad training data and data leakage are the core risks the blueprint expects you to know. Models can process logs and many languages, so the last two are simply false.

questions.question: An assistant with permission to run commands summarizes syslog messages. A message sent by a compromised host contains text telling the assistant to remove the ACL on the edge router. Which principle best limits the damage?
choices: Raise the syslog severity level
Use a larger language model
Send logs to the assistant in JSON instead of plain text
Give the assistant least privilege, treat what it reads as data, and require human approval for changes
questions.explanation: This is prompt injection: untrusted input trying to steer the AI. Read-only access by default and an approval step for any change keep a manipulated assistant from acting on the network.

questions.question: Why do vendor assistants retrieve your inventory, topology and configurations before answering a question?
choices: Retrieval lets the model run on the switch ASIC
A language model knows nothing about your specific network, so grounding it in your data makes answers relevant and reduces invented details
A new model must be trained for every question
Retrieval encrypts the question before it is sent
questions.explanation: This is retrieval-augmented generation: the platform supplies your real data with the question, so the model answers from facts about your network instead of general patterns alone.

questions.question: Which statement about how a large language model produces an answer is accurate?
choices: It looks up every answer in a verified database
It runs the commands it suggests to confirm they work
It generates likely text from patterns learned in training, and checks nothing unless the surrounding tool retrieves or verifies information
It always says when it is unsure
questions.explanation: An LLM predicts plausible text. Facts, lookups and verification come from the system around it, and it can sound equally confident whether it is right or wrong.

questions.question: Explain the difference between predictive and generative AI, with one network operations example of each.
questions.answer: Predictive AI analyzes historical and current data to detect, classify or forecast, such as flagging abnormal traffic or predicting that a link will run out of capacity. Generative AI creates new content from a prompt, such as summarizing an incident or drafting a configuration for review.
questions.explanation: Detect and forecast versus create: that one distinction answers most exam questions on this topic.

questions.question: An engineer deploys a configuration that an AI assistant drafted. Who is accountable for the change?
choices: The engineer and team who reviewed, approved and deployed it
The AI vendor
No one, because the AI wrote it
The device that accepted the configuration
questions.explanation: AI output is a draft. The people who verify, approve and deploy a change own it, which is why review and change control still apply.

questions.question: Why do AI features usually live in controllers and cloud platforms rather than on individual switches?
choices: Switches cannot generate any telemetry
AI is only licensed for wireless controllers
They need large amounts of centralized, structured data from many devices, plus significant compute
Individual switches have no CPU
questions.explanation: Baselines, correlation and language models need data from across the network and real compute power. Controllers and cloud platforms collect that data in one place; switches supply the telemetry.

questions.question: A model predicts next month's utilization of a WAN link as a percentage. Which kind of machine learning problem is this?
choices: Classification
Clustering
Regression
Reinforcement
questions.explanation: Predicting a number is regression. Classification predicts a category, clustering groups unlabeled items, and reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards.

questions.question: Which two are supervised learning problems? Choose two.
choices: Classifying flows as voice, video or backup, trained on captures labeled with the right application
Predicting next month's link utilization from months of recorded utilization
Grouping wireless clients by behavior when no categories exist
Improving a radio channel plan by trying settings and receiving a score
Flagging unusual logins when no attacks were ever labeled
questions.explanation: Both supervised problems learn from history that includes the answer: labeled flows (classification) and past utilization values (regression). Grouping without categories and flagging the unusual without labels are unsupervised, and learning from scores for actions is reinforcement learning.

questions.question: A link runs at 61 percent utilization and has grown a steady 3 percentage points per month. If the trend continues, after how many months does it first reach 85 percent?
questions.explanation: 85 minus 61 is 24 points, and 24 divided by 3 points per month is 8 months. That lead time is what makes forecasting useful: enough to order and install more capacity.

questions.question: Why is a capacity forecast most valuable months before a link actually fills up?
choices: Links cannot be monitored once they are busy
Forecasts become more accurate the further ahead they look
Upgrades such as new circuits take time to order and install, so warning in advance turns an outage into a planned change
The forecast automatically orders the new circuit
questions.explanation: The point of predicting is lead time. A static alert at 85 percent arrives when users already suffer; a forecast months ahead lets the team plan the upgrade. Forecasts get less certain, not more, the further out they look.

questions.question: Telemetry shows the error counters on this uplink rising every day for a week, while the link stays up and no alarm fires. What can a predictive model do with this that an up/down alert cannot?
questions.code:
dist-sw2# show interfaces TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1
TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  ...
     2847 input errors, 2791 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
  ...
choices: Nothing, because the interface is up and up
Prove the switch is under attack and block the neighbor
Rewrite the interface configuration to hide the errors
Flag the uplink as likely to fail, so the optic or fiber is checked and replaced in a maintenance window
questions.explanation: Steadily rising CRC errors usually mean a physical problem such as a dirty or failing optic or fiber. A model that has learned this pattern before past failures can warn while the link still works. An up/down alert only fires after the link fails.

questions.question: Endpoint analytics labels an unknown device "IP camera, 87 percent confidence". What is the sensible next step before applying the camera policy to it?
choices: Confirm the label (for example from its MAC vendor, switch port and owner), because a classification is a probability, not a certainty
Apply the policy immediately, because 87 percent is close enough
Block the device until it reaches 100 percent confidence
Retrain the model from scratch
questions.explanation: Classifiers output likelihoods. A strong label speeds up the work, but a wrong policy on a misclassified device can break something or open a hole, so confirm high-impact decisions. Waiting for 100 percent would mean waiting forever.

questions.question: How can machine learning flag malware inside TLS-encrypted traffic without decrypting it?
choices: It reads the payload after the TLS handshake finishes
It uses the private key that every switch keeps for each client
It learns patterns in flow metadata, such as packet lengths and timing early in the session, that differ between malware and normal applications
It blocks all encrypted traffic it cannot read
questions.explanation: Encrypted Traffic Analytics style detection classifies flows from metadata that stays visible: packet sizes, timing and handshake details. The content stays encrypted. Network devices do not hold clients' private keys, and blocking all TLS is not analytics.

questions.question: What distinguishes an AI agent from a chat assistant that only answers questions?
choices: An agent plans several steps and calls tools or APIs to act, so it needs scoped permissions and approval for changes
An agent never uses a language model
An agent can only read syslog messages
An agent runs on the switch ASIC
questions.explanation: Agents combine a model with tools: they can run commands through APIs, read the results and take the next step. That power is why they start with read-only access and need a human approval step before changing anything.

questions.question: Put the steps for safely using an AI-drafted configuration in order.
items: Read the draft and check addresses, masks, interfaces and direction
Check the current state of the device with show commands
Test the change in a lab or simulator
Deploy in a change window with a rollback plan
Verify counters and test traffic after deployment
questions.explanation: Understand the draft first, confirm it fits the real device, prove it in a lab, deploy with a way back, then verify the outcome. Each step catches mistakes the previous one could miss.

questions.question: Which three details make a prompt for a configuration draft much more useful? Choose three.
choices: The platform and software version
The exact goal and scope, such as VLANs and subnets
Constraints such as naming and where the change is applied
The words "please be accurate"
The device's enable secret, so the assistant can log in
questions.explanation: Platform, scope and constraints let the model produce something specific and checkable. Asking for accuracy changes nothing, and sharing secrets with an assistant is a data leak, not context.

questions.question: An assistant drafted this for the request "block Telnet from guest VLAN 50, allow everything else". After it is applied, guests lose all network access. Why?
questions.code:
ip access-list extended GUEST-NO-TELNET
 deny tcp 10.50.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq telnet
!
interface Vlan50
 ip access-group GUEST-NO-TELNET in
choices: The ACL must be applied out, not in, on an SVI
Telnet must be matched with eq 22
There is no permit statement, so the implicit deny at the end blocks all other guest traffic
Named ACLs cannot be applied to VLAN interfaces
questions.explanation: Every ACL ends with an implicit deny any. With only a deny line, the ACL blocks Telnet and then everything else. Adding permit ip any any after the deny fixes it. Applying a named extended ACL inbound on an SVI is valid, and Telnet is port 23.

questions.question: Why is it worth asking an assistant to list the assumptions behind its answer?
choices: Assumptions about interface names, software version or existing configuration are where errors hide, and a listed assumption can be checked
Listing assumptions makes the model run faster
Assumptions are only needed for predictive AI
The list proves the answer is correct
questions.explanation: A model fills gaps in the prompt with guesses. Seeing those guesses lets you confirm or correct each one against the real device. A list of assumptions makes checking easier; it does not prove anything by itself.

questions.question: A database server normally talks only to three internal app servers on two ports. Today it sends a small amount of traffic to an unfamiliar external address on an unusual port. Which approach is most likely to flag this?
choices: A static alert when the server sends more than 1 Gbps
Behavior-based anomaly detection learned from the server's normal peers and ports
A daily configuration backup
An SNMP poll of the server's CPU
questions.explanation: The volume is tiny, so a bandwidth threshold never fires. A baseline of who the server normally talks to, and on which ports, makes a new external peer stand out, which could indicate compromise or data exfiltration.

questions.question: Name four guardrails a team should put in place before AI output reaches production devices.
questions.answer: A qualified engineer reviews and approves the output; changes go through testing (lab or dry run), change control and a rollback plan; AI tools get least privilege, read-only first, with approval before any change; and suggestions, approvals and actions are logged.
questions.explanation: These are the same disciplines that make any automation safe, applied to a tool that can be confidently wrong.

questions.question: A manager says the new AI platform means the team no longer needs CCNA-level networking knowledge. Which response is most accurate?
choices: Agreed; AI output is reliable enough to apply without review
AI augments engineers, but networking knowledge is what lets them judge, verify and safely act on its output
AI has no practical use in network operations yet
Only generative AI needs human review; predictive AI never does
questions.explanation: AI speeds up analysis and drafting, but both predictive and generative systems make mistakes. Engineers who understand the network are the ones who can tell a good suggestion from a dangerous one.

questions.question: Match each data problem to the effect it has on an AI model.

pairs.left: Device clocks not synchronized with NTP
pairs.right: Events correlated in the wrong order

pairs.left: Baseline learned during a holiday week
Counters polled only every five minutes
A major new application goes live
pairs.right: Yesterday's normal becomes wrong until retraining

questions.explanation: Models learn from the data they are given. Skewed timestamps break correlation, unrepresentative history skews baselines, coarse samples hide bursts, and real change (drift) means the model must be retrained.
